newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana cocoa buyers ponder effects of dry spell.
newsitem.headline: Ghana cocoa buyers ponder effects of dry spell.

text.p: A harsh hot and dry spell in Ghana's cocoa producing areas in early 1997 left industry and exporters divided over its effects on the total 1996/97 crop.
"There is an effect but there is nothing to be excited about," a local manager for British chocolate maker Cadbury told Reuters.

"In 1995 the harmattan was much harsher," said Peter Grist, who has worked in Ghana since 1972. "I remember the rustling of the dry leaves - it was like the crackling of static electricity. This year that is not the case."
But some local traders said hot weather had cut into this year's production volumes, which private forecasters had put at 300,000-390,000 tonnes.
Cocoa Board director John Newman on March 10 put Ghana's total 1996/97 production at 330,000 tonnes against 403,800 in 1995/96.
Cumulative cocoa purchases announced by the state Cocobod marketing board to February 27 (week 20) totalled 294,216 tonnes against 329,509 around the same time last year.
Harmattan winds usually bring hot and dry weather to West Africa's cocoa producing areas in January.
This year's harmattan arrived late, extending well into February, and in some places March, before retreating northwards. Light occasional showers have begun to appear.
"Because of the prolonged dry and dusty (Harmattan desert wind) weather pods do not mature well ... beans do not loosen from the pod, they cluster," said one local trader.
Harvest volumes in Ashanti region had been good and those in Brong Ahafo were not bad, he added, but output from the key Western region had been disappointing.
Grist said bean sizes may have been smaller than might have been the case before the extended dry period, but he said overall quality in terms of bean size and humidity remained acceptable.

"The harmattan is slightly extended but not as harsh (as 1995)," he said. "The beans I see on the mats (for drying cocoa) now are all pretty good," he added, acknowledging that weak rains had been reflected in reduced soil water levels.
"That does not mean that the beans harvested now will be counted as mid-crop. They will still be main crop," he said.
This was because increasing plantings of hybrid cocoa in Ghana meant distinctions between main and mid-crop were lessening, he explained.
"In 1972, 90 percent of Ghana's cocoa was Amelonado cocoa. Now 65-70 percent is hybrid stock," he said.
"With amelonado you had two distinct cropping seasons," he added. "Hybrids have a tendency to produce crop all year around, albeit with peaks. But in between peaks it still dribbles in."
Forecasters expected 1996/97 output to be lower than 1995/96 because of poor pod-setting following heavy July and August rains and later evidence of blackpod in September.

One local trader put this year's main crop at 280,000 tonnes, with another 20,000 to 25,000 for the mid-crop. Others put total 1999/97 production, including mid-crop, at 340,000 tonnes. --Abidjan newsroom +225 21 90 90
